insider_note: This is the same t=Tan⁻¹x idea from answer 154, one derivative swapped for another — 1/√(1−x²) is the signature derivative of Sin⁻¹x, and the square root over t is just a fractional power of t once substituted.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Substitute t = Sin⁻¹x
steps.why: 1/√(1−x²) is the signature derivative of Sin⁻¹x, exactly as 1/(1+x²) is the signature derivative of Tan⁻¹x — the substitution removes the square root and the inverse function together.
common_mistakes: Not recognising 1/√(1−x²) as the derivative of Sin⁻¹x.
Treating √(Sin⁻¹x) as (Sin⁻¹x)² by mistake, confusing the square root with a square.
steps.memory_tip: 1/√(1−x²) is Sin⁻¹x's own derivative, the circular-function twin of 1/(1+x²) for Tan⁻¹x.

steps.label: Integrate and back-substitute for the final answer
steps.why: ∫dt/√t = ∫t⁻¹ᐟ²dt = 2√t + c by the power rule, and substituting t=Sin⁻¹x back in gives the final answer as a square root of an inverse sine.
common_mistakes: Missing the factor of 2 in ∫t⁻¹ᐟ²dt = 2t¹ᐟ², writing just √t.
Forgetting to substitute Sin⁻¹x back in for t.
steps.memory_tip: ∫dt/√t = 2√t — always a factor of 2, the same power-rule shortcut as ∫f′/√f dx from the LAQ chapter.
